intro: Being aware of the addictive potential of Xanax, there has been a significant amount of research dedicated to its use in the United States. In 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released a report that analyzed prescribed Xanax trends from 2014-2016.

The CDC shared that despite the known concerns of addiction, the prevalence of Xanax prescriptions has risen from 1996 to 2013. With this increase, the CDC observed an increase in emergency room visits and fatal overdoses associated with Xanax. While Xanax can be an effective medication for individuals who struggle with anxiety, it is an addictive substance with potentially dangerous and even fatal side effects.

sections.title: What is Xanax?
body: Xanax is classified as a Benzodiazepine, which acts similarly to a sedative. Xanax is one of the most commonly prescribed medications in the United States. Xanax can be prescribed for individuals who are living with anxiety disorders, most commonly Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Panic Disorder. For some, when taken as directed, Xanax can decrease anxiety symptoms and improve their quality of life.

body: When Xanax is abused, it is consumed in a manner other than what it was prescribed. For individuals who have a prescription, this can mean taking more than you were directed or taking your doses without the recommended time gap.

sections.title: Is Xanax Addictive?
body: Xanax can become addictive for individuals who abuse the medication, and those who are taking it to relieve mental health symptoms. Xanax can become physically addictive, which can include the development of physical dependency. With a physical dependency, an individual may become reliant on medication to maintain their day-to-day functioning.
Additionally, individuals who become addicted to Xanax often find themselves focused on it throughout the day. This can be time-consuming and have a negative impact on every aspect of our lives.
